tldr: We developed LEAP, a new solver that formulates trajectory optimization for legged robots with contacts as an augmented Lagrangian gradient flow rather than using Newton-type methods. It stably computes solutions that satisfy strict contact constraints while dramatically reducing sensitivity to the initial guess.
hero_caption: Tracking control in the MuJoCo simulator using reference trajectories generated by LEAP on two tasks: stepping-stone locomotion (left) and hurdle jumping (right). Across a variety of robots, from a 2-DoF planar hopper to the 32-DoF humanoid Talos, dynamic motions are realized without failure.
overview:
Planning motions where legged robots or manipulators interact with their environment requires solving a nonlinear, non-convex optimal control problem (OCP). However, contact dynamics constraints such as friction cones must hold at all times, making the problem exceptionally difficult as the number of joints increases. Existing state-of-the-art solvers like Crocoddyl and Aligator are based on Newton-type methods. As a result, they are extremely sensitive to the initial guess, suffering from a longstanding issue where poor initial estimates cause them to fail to converge or get trapped in local minima.

To address this, the authors turned to a fundamentally different approach: the gradient flow. By integrating a continuous descent equation along a virtual time axis (pseudo-time), a trajectory can be stably and gradually morphed toward the optimal solution, even starting from an initial guess far from it. However, conventional gradient flow methods handled constraints using quadratic penalties, which induced high stiffness in the solution and often caused numerical integration to break down. LEAP combines a Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar augmented Lagrangian with a primal–dual gradient flow, and further leverages a Bézier curve representation to establish a dedicated numerical integration scheme that integrates stably while strictly satisfying friction-cone constraints over continuous time.

Evaluated on a total of five robot platforms ranging from a 2-joint hopper to a 32-joint humanoid, LEAP was the only method that found feasible solutions across all 10 benchmark problems, which included difficult initial guesses and tasks where existing solvers failed. Furthermore, dynamic hopscotch motions were demonstrated on a real Unitree Go2 robot, proving that LEAP can stably generate trajectories with practical tracking performance.
contributions: Formulated a primal–dual gradient flow that satisfies the KKT conditions based on the Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar augmented Lagrangian, fundamentally eliminating the constraint violation penalty issues faced by conventional gradient flow methods.

Represented contact forces (wrenches) with Bézier curves and utilized the convex hull property of their control points to theoretically guarantee that friction-cone constraints are strictly satisfied across continuous time, including between discrete nodes.

Developed a linearly implicit integrator featuring a Gauss–Newton metric and a merit-based step controller, ensuring that the augmented Lagrangian numerically decreases monotonically even on stiff gradient flows.

Demonstrated superior robustness and computational efficiency over existing Newton-type solvers through simulations across five robots ranging from 2 to 32 joints, as well as hardware validation on a quadruped robot.

sections.heading: Why is contact-implicit trajectory optimization so difficult?
sections.summary: Trajectory optimization for robots with contacts faces three major challenges: nonlinear dynamics, friction-cone constraints that must hold at all times, and initial-guess sensitivity stemming from non-convexity. Existing Newton-type solvers are extremely sensitive to the initial guess and scale poorly with the number of joints. In this paper, we propose LEAP, a novel solver based on gradient flow.
sections.details:
When a robot walks or manipulates objects, its feet or end-effectors make contact with the ground or items. Planning such motions requires determining joint torques and contact forces so that the equations of motion are satisfied and contact forces stay strictly within the friction cone at all times. This is formulated as an optimal control problem (OCP) governed by hybrid dynamics.

Solving this problem is challenging primarily due to three reasons:
- Dynamics challenge: The equations of motion change discontinuously whenever contact modes switch.
- Constraint challenge: The friction cones and the equations of motion themselves are nonlinear and non-convex, and they must hold across all time instants, not just at a finite set of discrete points.
- Initial guess challenge: Because the entire problem is non-convex, it cannot be solved without a good initial guess (warm start). For new robots or unfamiliar motions, preparing such a good initial guess in advance is difficult.

Representative existing solvers such as Crocoddyl and Aligator are based on differential dynamic programming (DDP) or multiple shooting. While fast, they are fundamentally Newton-step algorithms. Consequently, they only work well in the "neighborhood of a solution"; with a poor initial guess, they diverge or get trapped in local minima. In addition, because they evaluate constraints only at discrete knot points, friction-cone constraints are often violated between points.

In contrast, the gradient flow, which deforms a trajectory toward an optimal solution in continuous pseudo-time, possesses global descent properties and is exceptionally robust to initial guesses. However, existing gradient flow studies handled constraints using simple penalty methods. When penalty parameters were increased to strictly enforce constraints, the equations became extremely stiff, leading to numerical integration breakdowns. LEAP is a new framework designed to overcome all of these challenges simultaneously.

sections.heading: Hybrid dynamics and polynomial representations satisfying constraints at all times
sections.summary: We formulate the robot's equations of motion for a pre-specified contact sequence alongside the optimal control problem to be solved. We also introduce the geometric properties of Bézier curves as a tool to guarantee contact wrench constraints over continuous time during trajectory discretization.
sections.details:
### II-A Robot Dynamics with Contact Sequences
Let $q(t)$ be the generalized coordinates of the robot and $v(t)$ be its velocities. While contact mode $j$ is active, the equations of motion are written as differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) with constraints. In this study, we consider a pre-specified sequence of contact mode transitions $(j_{0}, \ldots, j_{M-1})$ and switching times. Discontinuous velocity resets occur at impact based on a Newtonian collision model.

### II-B Contact Sequence Optimal Control Problem
The objective function is the sum of costs across all modes. The equality constraints $\mathcal{E}_i$ include the equations of motion, velocity resets, and boundary conditions, while the inequality constraints $\mathcal{I}_i$ include friction cones as well as state and input upper and lower bounds at each time instant. The critical requirement here is that these constraints must hold for "all times $t$" within the interval, rather than just at finite sampling points.

### II-C Polynomial Representations and the Magic of Bézier Curves
To represent continuous trajectories with a finite number of variables, each time interval is approximated using polynomials. For states and control inputs, Lagrange interpolation through Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto (CGL) nodes is used. For contact wrenches $\lambda(t)$, on the other hand, we adopt Bézier curves.
- Here is the key insight: A Bézier curve is a linear combination of Bernstein basis functions, which gives it the elegant geometric property that the entire curve is strictly contained within the convex hull of its control points.
- In other words, for a convex set like a friction cone, if a finite number of control points $\bar{\lambda}_b$ satisfy the friction cone, $\lambda(t)$ is guaranteed never to leave the friction cone at any moment in continuous time (Lemma 2). This fundamentally eliminates the risk of contact violations caused by discretization.

sections.heading: Formulating the OCP as a gradient flow via augmented Lagrangian
sections.summary: We transcribe the continuous optimization problem into a nonlinear programming problem and introduce the Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar augmented Lagrangian. By combining a primal gradient flow in pseudo-time with fixed multipliers and window-wise multiplier updates, we achieve convergence to exact KKT points.
sections.details:
### III-A Discretization (Transcription)
Each contact mode interval is treated as a polynomial element, forming the decision variable vector $z$. Costs are approximated via quadrature over CGL nodes, and dynamics and boundary conditions are enforced as equality constraints $\mathcal{E}_d$ on CGL nodes. Friction-cone constraints are enforced as inequality constraints $\mathcal{I}_d$ on the Bézier control points as described above.

### III-B Deriving the Gradient Flow
To solve the constrained optimization via gradient flow, we define the Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar (PHR) augmented Lagrangian $L_A(z, \gamma; \mu)$, where $\gamma$ represents the Lagrange multipliers and $\mu > 0$ denotes penalty parameters. A key strength of this formulation is that $L_A$ remains continuously differentiable ($C^1$) even with inequality constraints.

The optimization is designed as a two-time-scale primal–dual dynamic:
- Continuous flow in pseudo-time $s$ (Primal flow): With the multipliers $\gamma$ held fixed, the primal variables $z$ are updated continuously according to $\dot{z} = -\nabla_z L_A(z, \gamma; \mu)$. As a result, $L_A$ decreases monotonically along pseudo-time.
- Discrete multiplier updates (Dual jumps): At the end of each fixed pseudo-time interval (window), the multipliers $\gamma$ are updated based on constraint residuals.

Proposition 6 proves that the equilibrium points of this primal–dual flow coincide exactly with the KKT points (Karush–Kuhn–Tucker optimality conditions) of the original nonlinear program. Unlike pure penalty methods, exact constraint satisfaction is achieved without driving penalty parameters to infinity.

sections.heading: Tackling stiff equations: A dedicated integrator and adaptive mesh refinement
sections.summary: To address the stiffness of the gradient flow and Jacobian discontinuities during constraint transitions, we developed a linearly implicit integrator equipped with a Gauss–Newton metric. It adaptively controls step sizes while preserving monotonic descent of the objective function, and refines the mesh locally upon detecting inter-node errors.
sections.details:
### IV-A Linearly Implicit Step
As penalty weights increase, the gradient flow becomes stiff, leading to numerical divergence in explicit integrators. Fully implicit integrators, however, require solving nonlinear equations at every step, incurring substantial computational costs. LEAP therefore adopts a linearly implicit scheme that requires solving only a single linear system per step.
- Instead of calculating exact second derivatives, it uses a Gauss–Newton approximated Hessian $H$, which guarantees positive definiteness.
- To anticipate sudden changes when constraints activate or deactivate, a margin $\varepsilon_{\mathcal{A}}$ is added to the active constraint set.
- The resulting update step $\Delta z$ is mathematically equivalent to the Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) method with a damping factor, where the step size $h$ naturally functions as a trust-region radius.

### IV-B Acceptance Check and Step-Size Control
Standard ODE solvers determine step size based on local truncation error, but they tend to make incorrect decisions in optimization problems where vector fields have kinks due to constraint activation and deactivation. LEAP accepts steps purely from an optimization perspective—evaluating whether the augmented Lagrangian $L_A$ actually decreased—and scales the step size $h$ based on the ratio $\varrho$ between the actual decrease in $L_A$ and the model-predicted decrease. This strictly preserves the monotonic descent of $L_A$ even after numerical discretization.

### IV-C & IV-D Window Management and Feasibility Gates
At the end of a window, penalty parameters $\mu_t$ are selectively increased only for constraint groups that failed to reduce violations sufficiently. Avoiding uniform penalty increases prevents the solver from getting trapped in pathological local minima. Furthermore, constraint violations on nodes (node gate $G$) and continuous-time violations between nodes (fine grid violation $F$) are measured separately to determine the next action.

### IV-E Feasibility Flow and Adaptive $h$-Refinement
At the start of optimization, the process begins from a coarse initial guess constructed simply by linearly interpolating boundary poses. It first runs a "feasibility flow" that ignores the cost function and minimizes the sum of squared constraint violations, bringing the trajectory into a broadly feasible region. Subsequently, if constraints are satisfied at the nodes but violations remain between them ($F > \mathrm{tol}$), intervals with large violations are bisected ($h$-refinement) based on Dörfler marking, automatically refining the polynomial mesh.

sections.heading: Large-scale simulation comparisons across five robot platforms
sections.summary: We compared LEAP against Crocoddyl and Aligator across five robots, ranging from a 2-DoF hopper to a 32-DoF humanoid, on two challenging tasks: stepping-stone locomotion and hurdle jumping. LEAP was the only method capable of generating trackable trajectories to target states across all 10 benchmark problems.
sections.details:
### V-A Experimental Setup
For a fair comparison, all solvers were evaluated on the same machine (AMD EPYC 7742, 12 cores per method) using identical cost functions, boundary conditions, and initial guesses.
- Target robots: Five platforms were tested: a planar hopper (2 joints), Unitree Go2 (12 joints), H1 (19 joints), G1 (29 joints), and PAL Robotics Talos (32 joints).
- Tasks: A total of 10 problems comprising stepping-stone locomotion (irregular step heights and placements) and hurdle jumping (requiring whole-body collision avoidance).
- Evaluation metric: Beyond raw numerical outputs from the solvers, trajectories were tracked in the high-fidelity physics simulator MuJoCo using a whole-body inverse dynamics controller (simulated rollout). Success was rigorously evaluated based on whether final terminal pose and foot placement errors cleared predefined thresholds (Table I).

### V-B Convergence and Compute Time (Table II, Table III)
Under an optimization time limit of 14,400 seconds (4 hours), Crocoddyl succeeded in finding trackable solutions for only 7 out of 10 problems, and Aligator succeeded in 8. In contrast, LEAP succeeded on all 10 problems.
- In high-DoF, highly demanding tasks (e.g., G1 hurdle jump), Crocoddyl broke down midway and Aligator timed out, whereas LEAP found a clean solution in 3,382 seconds.
- In terms of normalized terminal pose error (Table III), LEAP achieved the lowest error in 9 out of 10 problems, delivering trajectories that reached target goals far more accurately than baseline methods.

### V-C Solution Quality Across Compute Budgets (Figure 2)
We investigated at what stage trackable trajectories emerged when compute time was truncated early. LEAP was the fastest to cross the trackable threshold (normalized error $\le 1.0$) in 7 out of 10 problems. Driven by the initial feasibility flow and smooth gradient flow deformation, LEAP proved capable of discovering viable motions early, even under modest compute budgets.

sections.heading: Dynamic motion validation on a real quadruped robot
sections.summary: A dynamic "hopscotch" motion involving complex foot-contact and jumping patterns generated by LEAP was executed on a real Unitree Go2 robot. Combined with a controller designed to bridge the sim-to-real gap, the robot achieved high-precision tracking with centimeter-level accuracy.
sections.details:
### VI-A Hardware Setup
Experiments were conducted using a Unitree Go2 EDU (12 DoF). Joint angles and base orientation were acquired from onboard sensors, while base position was measured with a Vicon motion capture system.

### VI-B Controller and System Identification
To execute references obtained from trajectory optimization, modeling errors were reduced through system identification. Furthermore, to address residual dynamic discrepancies, an RL-based tracking controller trained with domain randomization (modeled after Deep Tracking Control) was deployed alongside the planner. LEAP supplied the feedforward whole-body trajectory, while the low-level controller applied real-time feedback corrections.

### VI-C Results
The robot successfully executed the hopscotch routine on real hardware, which involved rapid contact mode transitions including forward jumping, landing on diagonal leg pairs, and wide four-leg stances. Root-mean-square (RMS) tracking error was 0.0682 rad for joint positions and remained within centimeters for base positions (0.0461 m surge, 0.0253 m sway, and 0.0211 m heave). This verified that the optimized trajectories strictly conformed to the physical constraints of real hardware.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: LEAP is a new trajectory optimization method integrating augmented Lagrangian primal–dual gradient flows, Bézier wrench representations, and a dedicated linearly implicit integrator. Its high robustness and constraint-satisfaction capabilities on high-DoF robots have been demonstrated in both simulation and real-world experiments.
sections.details:
In this paper, we proposed LEAP, a new trajectory optimization method for robots with pre-specified contact sequences.
- By uniting pseudospectral collocation with a two-time-scale PHR augmented Lagrangian gradient flow, we established a framework that searches for KKT points without relying on Newton-type steps.
- Bézier curve representations mathematically guarantee friction-cone compliance across continuous time, while a Gauss–Newton linearly implicit integrator reliably tames the stiffness of the gradient flow.
- Across 10 benchmarks on five robot platforms, LEAP achieved a 100% success rate, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods (Crocoddyl, Aligator), and demonstrated precise dynamic jumping motions on a physical Unitree Go2.

The code will be made public upon final acceptance of the paper, offering a promising new standard tool for motion generation on high-DoF robots with contacts.

takeaways: Gradient flow provides a powerful paradigm that overcomes the severe initial-guess sensitivity inherent in conventional Newton-type solvers.
Representing contact forces (wrenches) with Bézier curves guarantees continuous-time friction-cone satisfaction across intervals simply by treating control points as convex inequality constraints.

To handle the stiffness and discontinuities of augmented Lagrangians, a dedicated linearly implicit integrator incorporating optimization merit checks is far more effective than standard off-the-shelf ODE solvers.
Evaluating solvers based on closed-loop tracking success in high-fidelity simulators, rather than merely measuring node residuals, is practically essential.
limitations: Contact sequences and switching timings must be specified in advance; autonomous discovery of contact sequences is not addressed.
Although each step requires solving only a single linear system, current compute times remain too long for real-time model predictive control (MPC) loops running at tens of milliseconds.

Non-convex geometric constraints, such as obstacle avoidance and self-collisions, cannot easily leverage continuous-time guarantees like Bézier curves, relying instead on mesh refinement to mitigate inter-node violations.
